implementation_notes: Modern C++ writes the monitor by hand from the standard library: a std::mutex member is the monitor lock and std::condition_variable the monitor condition, with std::unique_lock/std::scoped_lock providing the Scoped Locking idiom so the lock is released on every exit path. The predicate overload of condition_variable::wait replaces the hand-written loop and handles spurious wakeups; notify_one/notify_all correspond to signal/broadcast, and std::jthread with stop tokens can make an indefinite wait cancellable. Use condition_variable_any only when the lock is not a std::mutex, and split interface methods from implementation methods so intra-object calls never re-lock.
pitfalls: std::condition_variable only works with std::unique_lock<std::mutex>; using it with another lockable type requires condition_variable_any, and a notify without holding the mutex must not precede publishing the state change.

A condition variable carries no state: notify_one before any waiter arrives is a lost wakeup unless the predicate already reflects the change, which is exactly what the predicated wait overload enforces.
Do not block, allocate heavily or call foreign code while holding the mutex, and do not paper over intra-object re-locking with std::recursive_mutex - the Thread-Safe Interface split is the fix.

variants.name: Executor/strand serialisation without a lock
variants.idiom_name: strand<> + bind_executor: every handler of the object runs on one strand
variants.implementation_notes: Where the object is only reached from asynchronous handlers, the monitor lock is replaced by confinement to a strand: a strand is a strictly sequential invocation of handlers, so every method becomes a handler posted through boost::asio::bind_executor(strand, ...) and no two of them ever run concurrently. There is no monitor lock and no condition variable - a method that must wait for the state to change re-posts itself or resumes a continuation instead of blocking a thread, which is what makes this form usable inside an event loop. It realises the same guarantee (one method at a time inside the object) through scheduling rather than mutual exclusion; choose it when the surrounding code is already Asio-based.
pitfalls: A strand only serialises handlers that actually go through it: a direct call, a different executor or an unbound completion handler escapes the serialisation silently.
Handlers must not block: a blocking call inside a strand stalls the io_context and every object bound to that executor, which is why waits become continuations.
The object must outlive every posted handler (shared_from_this or explicit lifetime management), and all intermediate handlers of a composed operation must use the same strand.

variants.name: ACE wrapper facades (the POSA2-era C++ realisation)
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's original C++ home: POSA2 and the pattern paper document this structure with ACE wrapper facades, where a class holds a Thread_Mutex as its monitor lock and Thread_Condition objects as monitor conditions, each interface method wraps its body in Guard<Thread_Mutex>, forwards to non-synchronised implementation methods and waits in a predicate loop. ACE_Message_Queue is the production version of exactly this shape, and Strategized Locking can parameterise the synchronisation policy (MT_SYNCH versus NULL_SYNCH) over the same class template. Choose it only when ACE is already in the stack; otherwise std::mutex/std::condition_variable replace it one to one.
pitfalls: ACE condition variables are bound to a specific mutex wrapper: mixing mutex types, or signalling from outside the guard's scope, breaks the monitor without a compiler error.
The ACE stack is C++03-era and heavyweight; without its service configuration and reactor layers the standard library gives the same structure with less machinery.
